overview: Green Cross Health is now a pure-play New Zealand community pharmacy operator, running a network of roughly 320 pharmacies under the Unichem and Life Pharmacy franchise/ownership brands. Until 31 July 2026 the company also owned The Doctors, New Zealand's largest general-practice/urgent-care network (65 clinics, ~413,000 enrolled patients), but this Medical division was sold to Tend Health for NZ$270 million and the sale completed on 31 July 2026, leaving GXH a smaller, single-segment retail-pharmacy business sitting on a large cash balance with no committed use.

business_model.summary: GXH earns dispensary revenue from Te Whatu Ora (Health New Zealand)-funded prescription dispensing plus front-of-store retail (health, beauty, wellness, OTC) through a network of pharmacies that are a mix of wholly owned stores, majority/partly-owned subsidiaries, equity-accounted associates and franchise arrangements (franchise fees, supplier/promotional income and loyalty-programme monetisation via the 2.1 million-member Living Rewards scheme). Because New Zealand's Medicines Act has historically required pharmacies to be majority pharmacist-owned, GXH's growth model has relied on partial ownership stakes and franchise relationships with pharmacist-shareholders rather than 100% acquisition -- which is why ~21% of group post-tax profit is attributable to non-controlling interests rather than to GXH shareholders. Government deregulation of these ownership rules (Medical Products Bill / Medicines Amendment Act 2025) is now underway and could change this structure, for better (more consolidation flexibility for GXH) or worse (it also removes the barrier that has kept large non-pharmacist discount chains like Chemist Warehouse out of full ownership).

revenue_streams.name: Pharmacy retail and dispensary
revenue_streams.trend: growing (dispensing volume flat, revenue mix-driven by high-cost drugs)

revenue_streams.name: Other pharmacy services (franchise fees, supplier income)
Medical services (The Doctors) -- DIVESTED 31-Jul-2026, no longer part of the business

business_model.note_on_mix: FY2026 (year to 31-Mar-2026, the last full year reported) still included Medical: Pharmacy segment revenue $380.2m (70% of group) vs Medical segment revenue $165.8m (30% of group). Post-completion, 100% of GXH's ~$380m revenue base is pharmacy. Pharmacy segment profit was $22.245m in FY2026 versus Medical's $26.042m -- GXH has therefore divested the more profitable of its two former divisions, not the weaker one.
business_model.customer_type: B2C retail/patients at point of sale, with government (Te Whatu Ora / PHARMAC Community Pharmacy Services Agreement) as the largest single funding counterparty for dispensing and clinical services

main_competitors: Chemist Warehouse (Australian-owned discount chain, ~70 NZ stores at end-2025, ~66% of it claims Australian retail pharmacy market share benchmark, targeting 140 NZ stores within 5-10 years)
Independent/community pharmacies and smaller franchise groups (Amcal, Care Pharmacy and unaffiliated independents)
Supermarkets and grocery chains (Countdown/Woolworths NZ, Pak'nSave, New World) encroaching on front-of-store health & beauty and OTC
Bargain/variety retailers (The Warehouse, Kmart) for OTC and wellness categories
competitive_position.market_position: Green Cross Health, via Unichem and Life Pharmacy, is one of New Zealand's two largest pharmacy networks by store count (~320 stores) and the incumbent scale player, but it is losing share and margin to Chemist Warehouse's aggressive, price-led expansion; management itself has acknowledged Chemist Warehouse has 'had a bit of an impact on margins'.

moat_factors.description: Two long-established, trusted retail brands (Unichem, Life Pharmacy) with national coverage and a 2.1 million-member loyalty programme (Living Rewards) support customer retention, but scale alone has not stopped margin compression from discount competition.

The historical Medicines Act requirement for majority pharmacist ownership and a 5-pharmacy ownership cap has structurally protected the community-pharmacy model from full-scale corporate/discount consolidation. This is now being deregulated (Medical Products Bill/Medicines Amendment Act 2025), removing a protection that has underpinned GXH's franchise-based moat and potentially enabling more aggressive expansion by discount operators.

Deep, long-standing integration with the Community Pharmacy Services Agreement and PHARMAC dispensing/service-fee framework, plus the ability to deliver newly funded clinical services (vaccinations, minor ailments, emergency contraception, extended pharmacist scope) through 170 Care & Advice Health Hubs -- a service-based differentiation Chemist Warehouse cannot easily replicate at the same clinical depth.
Patients can and do switch pharmacies for price on repeat, low-touch dispensing; loyalty programmes provide only modest retention friction.

Chemist Warehouse's centralised, high-volume, low-margin discount model appears structurally lower-cost than GXH's franchise/partial-ownership network, and Chemist Warehouse is actively lobbying for centralised automated dispensing robotics that would widen this gap further.

weaknesses: Structurally thin dispensary margins, further compressed by rising volumes of high-cost/low-margin specialty medicines (e.g., Wegovy, funded cancer treatments) that lift revenue but shrink gross margin
Loss of the more profitable, faster-growing Medical division leaves a smaller, lower-margin, more competitively pressured earnings base
~21% of post-tax profit accrues to non-controlling interests, meaning reported group earnings materially overstate what flows to GXH shareholders
No large-scale online/omni-channel advantage yet versus increasingly digital-savvy discount and supermarket competitors, though a new app and shoppable Unichem website were launched in FY2026
Heavy reliance on a single government funder (Te Whatu Ora/PHARMAC) for a large share of dispensing economics

growth_drivers: Government extension of pharmacist scope of practice and funded clinical services (from 2 June 2026: extended range of funded medicines without prescription, emergency contraception funding, minor ailment consultations) -- directly monetisable through the 170-site Care & Advice Health Hub network
Continued rollout of Care & Advice Health Hubs, vaccinations (330,000 administered in FY2026) and other higher-margin clinical/advisory services to offset dispensary margin compression
Digital investment: new Unichem/Life Pharmacy app (200+ pharmacies onboarded), shoppable Unichem website (click & collect, home delivery), integrated online booking
'Beauty by Life' premium retail concept expansion and 'Feel Good, Pay Less' value range to defend both premium and price-sensitive customer segments

Potential deployment of Medical-sale proceeds (up to NZ$270m gross, before net debt/working-capital adjustments) into pharmacy network acquisitions, greenfield stores, or technology/automation to compete with Chemist Warehouse's cost base
Possible capital return (special dividend or return of capital) directly boosting per-share value if the Board does not find sufficiently accretive reinvestment opportunities in pharmacy

business.description: Chemist Warehouse plans to double its NZ store count from ~70 to ~140 within 5-10 years and is lobbying government for centralised automated dispensing and easier pharmacist immigration, directly targeting the mass/value segment GXH also serves; already opening stores adjacent to existing Unichem sites.

The Medical Products Bill/Medicines Amendment Act 2025 is removing the requirement that pharmacies be majority pharmacist-owned and the 5-pharmacy ownership cap. This could let discount or corporate chains consolidate more aggressively, eroding a structural protection GXH's franchise model has relied on -- though it could equally let GXH itself acquire more of its partly-owned network.

business.risk: Dispensary margin compression from high-cost drugs
business.description: Growth in dispensing of high-value, low-margin medicines (e.g., Wegovy, funded cancer treatments) inflates revenue while compressing gross margin -- a trend management explicitly flagged in FY2026.

With Medical divested, GXH is a smaller, single-segment company (~$380m revenue vs ~$546m combined) more exposed to pharmacy-specific cyclical and competitive swings, having given up the segment that grew profit 33% in FY2026.

The Group consolidates 36 of 53 subsidiaries where it holds 50% or less of profit shares (ownership ranges 24%-100%); NCI took $5.5m (~21%) of FY2026 post-tax profit, meaning per-share value must be assessed on attributable earnings, not consolidated group profit.

financial.risk: Undecided use of NZ$270m sale proceeds
financial.description: As of 11 August 2026, the Board has made no public commitment on whether proceeds will fund a capital return, pharmacy acquisitions, debt reduction, or a combination -- creating material valuation uncertainty and capital-allocation execution risk (value-destructive diversification cannot be ruled out).

financial.risk: Large lease liabilities functioning as quasi-debt
financial.description: FY2026 IFRS16 lease depreciation was $15.392m and lease interest $8.240m -- both far larger than non-lease D&A ($5.162m) and non-lease interest expense ($1.592m). Lease principal repayments ($13.752m cash in FY2026) are a real, recurring cash cost that must be deducted when assessing owner free cash flow; total lease liabilities of $105.0m (current $13.751m + non-current $91.261m) sit alongside only $19.8m of bank borrowings.

Auditor KPMG flagged goodwill impairment as a key audit matter: $86.8m Pharmacy and $77.3m Medical goodwill (Medical goodwill will now transfer with the sale), with the market capitalisation deficit versus book value at balance date cited as an impairment indicator.
Net assets per share $1.33 but net tangible assets per share only $0.08 -- book value is overwhelmingly goodwill/intangibles, offering little tangible-asset support if trading deteriorates.

regulatory.description: A large share of Pharmacy division economics flows through Te Whatu Ora/PHARMAC dispensing fees and the Community Pharmacy Services Agreement. Any reduction, freeze, or restructuring of government funding rates would directly hit dispensary economics with limited offsetting flexibility.

As above -- covered under business risks but has a distinct regulatory-process dimension: the Medical Products Bill is still moving through the legislative process, so the ultimate rules (and transition timing) remain uncertain.

Health New Zealand's approval of a new Primary Health Organisation, Community Care Limited (commencing 1 July 2026), was designed for the (now sold) Medical division; GXH's remaining pharmacy business has separate, less concentrated funding relationships.

macro.description: Front-of-store retail (health & beauty, wellness) is discretionary and sensitive to a soft NZ consumer/retail environment; management described itself as only 'cautiously optimistic' about the 2026 retail recovery.

Low direct balance-sheet debt (gearing 9.4% at FY2026, net cash position of $8.6m pre-sale) limits rate sensitivity, but the very large IFRS16 lease book means the effective (lease-inclusive) obligation base is materially higher and modestly rate-sensitive via incremental borrowing rate assumptions on new/renewed leases.
Wages and salaries were the single largest cost line ($195.5m, 36% of group operating expenditure) in FY2026; pharmacist and healthcare labour cost inflation is an ongoing margin pressure.

macro_factors.industry_outlook: NZ community pharmacy is a low-growth, government-funding-dependent, increasingly price-competitive retail-plus-clinical-services industry. Government policy is actively expanding pharmacists' clinical scope (a tailwind for higher-margin services) while simultaneously deregulating ownership structures (a headwind for incumbent moats).
macro_factors.cyclicality: Low to moderate -- prescription dispensing is defensive/non-discretionary, but front-of-store retail and beauty/wellness spend are more cyclical and consumer-discretionary.
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: Low on traditional debt (minimal bank borrowings, net cash pre-sale), moderate via the large IFRS16 lease book and incremental borrowing rate assumptions.

recent_developments.event: FY2026 (year to 31 March 2026) results: Group revenue $546.0m (+4.2%), Operating Profit (EBIT) $45.3m, NPAT attributable to shareholders $20.4m (+27.7%), final dividend 5.5cps declared (total FY26 dividends 8.5cps), Pharmacy segment profit $22.2m, Medical segment profit $26.0m (+33%).

GXH announced a conditional sale and purchase agreement to sell its Medical division (The Doctors: 65 clinics, >400,000 enrolled patients) to Tend Health for NZ$270 million, subject to net debt/working-capital adjustments; Board said it would consider options for proceeds including reinvestment in pharmacy growth and/or a distribution or return of capital to shareholders.

Health New Zealand extension of pharmacy services for common health conditions took effect, expanding the range of medicines pharmacists can assess and supply without a prescription and funding emergency contraception consultations for women under 25 -- a direct tailwind for GXH's Care & Advice Health Hub model.

Health New Zealand approval for GXH's new Primary Health Organisation, Community Care Limited, took effect (relevant to the now-divested Medical division; 54 practices joined ahead of the Tend Health sale completing).
Shareholders approved the Medical division sale at the annual/special meeting, with 99.82% of votes in favour.
Sale of the Medical division to Tend Health completed. GXH is now a pure-play pharmacy retailer. No decision on use of proceeds has been announced as of 11 August 2026.

Chemist Warehouse continued aggressive New Zealand expansion (store count ~70 by end-2025, network sales growth of over 20% year-on-year, targeting ~140 stores within 5-10 years), including opening stores directly adjacent to existing Unichem locations; GXH management has publicly acknowledged margin impact but says its differentiation is value plus clinical care and advice.

guidance.as_of: FY2026 Annual Result, 29 May 2026 (pre-dates Medical division sale completion)

items.notes: GXH's results presentations use qualitative 'Future Focus' priorities rather than numeric guidance. No FY2027 revenue, EBIT or NPAT targets have been published, and none would be comparable to FY2026 given the Medical division divestment restates the earnings base entirely.

1 June 2026 announcement stated the Board 'will consider options for the most efficient use of the sale proceeds, which may include retaining some proceeds to invest in the growth of the Pharmacy division and a distribution or return of capital to shareholders.' No further public update on this decision could be found as of the date of this analysis -- this is explicitly unresolved, not merely unquantified.

items.target: Expand Care & Advice Health Hubs; differentiated brands/products; omni-channel digital engagement; leverage network scale; workforce productivity, margin and occupancy cost management
items.notes: Consistent with FY2026 'Pharmacy Future Focus' priorities disclosed in the FY2026 Annual Report and results presentation.

guidance.management_commentary: Management described itself as 'cautiously optimistic regarding the recovery of the New Zealand economy and the outlook for retail' in 2026, and reiterated intent to keep advocating for extended pharmacist scope of practice and sustainable community pharmacy funding models. No numeric FY2027 targets, and critically no capital-return decision, had been disclosed as of 11 August 2026 -- the single most important open question for the investment case.

capital_allocation_analysis.context: GXH shares on issue: 143,834,147. Share price 11-Aug-2026: NZ$1.95, implying a market capitalisation of approximately NZ$280m. The Medical division alone was sold for NZ$270m (before adjustments), meaning the market is effectively valuing the entire retained pharmacy business plus net cash at only marginally more than the cash proceeds themselves -- a striking, headline-grabbing disconnect that is the crux of the investment case.
capital_allocation_analysis.scenario_framing: This cannot be resolved definitively without knowing (a) the actual net cash proceeds after debt/working-capital adjustments and transaction costs, and (b) what the Board decides to do with them, both of which are unknown as of this analysis. Two illustrative, non-verified scenarios: (1) if most of the ~$270m (less adjustments, tax and costs) is retained as cash and the market is pricing that cash near face value, then the market is implicitly valuing the standalone Pharmacy business (FY2026 segment profit $22.2m before minority interests) at a very low, possibly close to zero or even negative, multiple -- which would be unusually cheap for a defensive, government-funded dispensing business, but could reflect the sale not yet being reflected in the share register/price or the market pricing in the Chemist Warehouse/deregulation risks discussed above. (2) Conversely, if the market has already priced in an assumed near-full capital return, the residual implied value being paid for the pharmacy operating business could be more normal -- in which case the stock offers little further upside from a 'sum of the parts' surprise and is instead a bet on execution of the pharmacy strategy alone.
capital_allocation_outcomes_to_watch: Full or majority special dividend / pro-rata return of capital to shareholders -- likely the most value-transparent outcome, though NZ tax treatment differs: a fully imputed special dividend carries imputation credits usable by NZ resident shareholders (reducing effective tax cost), whereas a formal 'return of capital' (share capital reduction) can in some circumstances be treated as a dividend for NZ tax purposes unless structured to qualify for capital treatment -- shareholders should not assume a return of capital is automatically tax-free; the actual tax character will depend on how the Board structures the distribution and IRD guidance/rulings obtained.

Reinvestment in pharmacy network expansion or acquisitions (e.g., buying out non-controlling interests in existing partly-owned pharmacies, greenfield stores, automation/dispensing robotics to compete with Chemist Warehouse's cost base) -- could be value-accretive if disciplined, but is unproven and carries execution and overpayment risk given GXH already trades on goodwill-heavy multiples.

Debt/lease reduction -- GXH already carries low bank debt (gearing 9.4%, near net cash pre-sale) so this is a lower-value use of proceeds versus the other options, though buying out expensive lease commitments or NCI stakes is a plausible variant.

Value-destructive diversification (e.g., stepping outside core pharmacy into adjacent but unproven healthcare verticals) -- cannot be ruled out and is the classic risk for a company that has just banked a large, unallocated cash pile; investors should watch closely for how disciplined the Board is in any reinvestment announcements.
This is unambiguously a 'value trap or catalyst' situation: the outcome for shareholders depends almost entirely on a Board capital-allocation decision that has not yet been made public.

bull_case: The market capitalisation (~NZ$280m) is only marginally above the gross NZ$270m Medical division sale price, suggesting the retained pharmacy business plus cash could be significantly undervalued if a large portion of proceeds is confirmed as cash/near-cash and eventually returned or redeployed productively

A likely special dividend or return of capital would crystallise value quickly and transparently for shareholders, and NZ imputation credits could make a fully-imputed distribution tax-efficient for resident holders
Post-sale GXH is a simpler, more focused, dispensary-and-retail pharmacy business with reduced execution complexity versus running two very different regulated healthcare segments

Government policy is actively expanding pharmacists' funded clinical scope of practice (vaccinations, minor ailments, contraception, extended prescribing), a direct, monetisable tailwind for the 170-site Care & Advice Health Hub network

Defensive, non-discretionary dispensing revenue base with government (Te Whatu Ora/PHARMAC) as a stable long-term funding counterparty, combined with low starting financial leverage (ex-lease) after the sale
bear_case: The Board has made no public commitment to return capital -- proceeds could instead be redeployed into unproven or lower-return pharmacy acquisitions/expansion, or even value-destructive diversification, in which case the current price already reflects fair value for a smaller, lower-margin retained business

GXH has divested its more profitable and faster-growing division (Medical, FY2026 segment profit $26.0m, +33% YoY) and kept the less profitable one (Pharmacy, $22.2m, +4%), shrinking both the earnings base and the growth trajectory of the remaining business

Chemist Warehouse's well-funded, aggressive NZ expansion (targeting a doubling of its store count) is structurally compressing dispensary and retail margins, and looming deregulation of pharmacist-ownership rules could remove a historical protective barrier for incumbents like GXH

Reported group profit overstates shareholder value: ~21% of FY2026 post-tax profit accrued to non-controlling interests given GXH's partial-ownership/franchise structure across the bulk of its subsidiaries

Large IFRS16 lease obligations (>$105m total lease liabilities, ~$22m/year combined lease depreciation and interest) function as quasi-debt and consume real cash via lease principal repayments, meaning reported EBIT/NPAT overstate free cash flow available to shareholders; the balance sheet is also intangible-heavy (net tangible assets per share only $0.08 vs net assets per share $1.33), leaving thin tangible support if trading or goodwill assumptions deteriorate
